raw_response:
I'll think this through the way I always do — crop by crop, starting from what I did last year.

My land is 9.2 mu. The main part, about 5 mu, I rotate cabbage in spring, then Chinese cabbage in autumn, then spinach through the cold months. The other 4.2 mu I split into three small plots for chili, eggplant, and kidney bean in the summer. That is how I kept it last year and the market was alright, so I will do the same.

For fertilizer, I buy what the dealer in town sells. Compound fertilizer comes in 40 kg bags. For cabbage and Chinese cabbage, I put 2 bags of compound in the ground before planting on each mu, then topdress with urea — about half a bag, maybe a bit more — when the heads start forming. Those two crops eat a lot. Spinach does not need as much, one bag of compound is enough, and a small handful of urea when it greens up.

Chili and eggplant I treat almost the same as cabbage — they stay in the ground a long time so they need feeding. Kidney bean I do not give much nitrogen. My old neighbor always said beans make their own, and I have seen it — if you give them too much they grow leaves, not pods. So just a bag of compound and that is it.

Water: I have the well, so I water when the soil gets dry. Cabbage and Chinese cabbage I water maybe 5 or 6 times each. Spinach in winter only 2 or 3 times. Chili and eggplant drink a lot in summer — 7 or 8 times.

Pesticides I use when I see worms or aphids, not before. Cabbage worms and Chinese cabbage worms come every year, I will spray 3 times each. Eggplant gets those red mites so I spray 4 times. Kidney bean 2 times is enough.

I plough the land properly before cabbage and Chinese cabbage — turn it deep with the tractor man from the village. For spinach I just rotary because the cabbage is just out. Chili, eggplant, bean I plough once at the start.

Seed — I buy hybrid cabbage and Chinese cabbage seed, the dealer says it is better and my neighbors use it. Spinach and kidney bean I save my own or buy the cheap kind, they grow fine.
